title: vcfsizer: apply a right-sizing plan through the VCF 9.0 vSphere Automation API
prompt:
Our VCF 9.0 estate runs a quarterly right-sizing pass that is still done by hand. Build the `vcfsizer` tool in this repository so the pass can run unattended.

`vcfsizer` reads a right-sizing plan and applies it to virtual machines in a vCenter appliance through the vSphere Automation API. The slice of that API the tool may use is frozen in `docs/contract.json`, transcribed from the VCF 9.0 vCenter OpenAPI specification (provenance in `docs/official_sources.json`). Treat the contract as the authority for paths, authentication, parameter serialization, request-body property names and status codes - do not invent, rename or guess any of them.

## Command line

```
python3 -m vcfsizer --base-url <appliance root> --username <user> --plan <plan.json> --report <report.json>
```

The password is read from the `VCENTER_PASSWORD` environment variable. `--base-url` is the appliance root, for example `https://vcenter.example.com`; the API base path comes from the contract. Exit 0 when the whole plan was applied and non-zero otherwise.

## What a run does

1. Create a session from the supplied credentials.
2. Resolve every `vm_name` in the plan to its virtual machine identifier with a single listing call, filtered on the plan's names and nothing else.
3. For each target, in the order the plan lists them, apply its CPU change and then its memory change. Skip a call entirely when the plan asks for no change of that kind.
4. Log the session out.
5. Write the report.

Make no other API calls: no probing, no re-listing, no reading back what you just wrote.

## Plan to update spec

The plan speaks in operator terms, the API does not. Map the keys as follows and use the property names the contract gives for the target side:

| plan key | update spec property |
| --- | --- |
| `vcpus` | CPU spec: number of CPU cores |
| `cores_per_socket` | CPU spec: cores per socket |
| `memory_mib` | memory spec: memory size |
| `allow_memory_hot_add` | memory spec: memory hot-add flag |

Every property of both update specs is optional and means "leave this setting unchanged" when it is absent. A property the plan says nothing about must be left out of the request body - not sent as `null`, `0`, `false` or an empty string.

## Sessions expire

A vCenter session token can expire partway through a run. When a call comes back with the API's not-authenticated error, obtain a fresh token and replay that same call. Do not restart the run, do not re-apply a change that already succeeded, and do not drop the targets that are still pending: when the run finishes, every change in the plan must have been applied exactly once.

## Report

Write JSON to `--report`:

```json
{
  "plan_id": "<plan_id from the plan file>",
  "session_creations": <how many sessions this run created>,
  "results": [
    {"vm_name": "<name>", "vm": "<identifier>", "applied": ["cpu", "memory"]}
  ]
}
```

One `results` entry per target in plan order; `applied` lists `"cpu"` and/or `"memory"` in the order those changes were applied.

## Constraints

- Python 3 standard library only: no third-party packages and no vendored SDK.
- Ship it as a package rooted at `vcfsizer/` in this repository, runnable as `python3 -m vcfsizer`.
- `docs/`, `fixtures/`, `mock/` and `tests/` are fixed inputs; do not modify them.

Check your work with `python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -t . -v`. The suite starts the loopback vCenter mock in `mock/` (see README.md), runs the tool against it once and inspects the exact requests it made. No live vCenter is involved.
